subject: Critical Thinking
title: The Trolley Problem: The Dilemma That Won't Die
description: Learn The Trolley Problem: The Dilemma That Won't Die in one minute.

hook.text: A runaway trolley will kill 5 people. You can pull a lever to divert it, killing 1 instead.

buildup.text: Philippa Foot (1967) created the trolley problem to test moral intuitions about killing vs. letting die.

discovery.text: Variation: instead of a lever, you push a large man off a bridge to stop the trolley. Same math, but most people refuse.

twist.text: The difference: personal physical violence feels wrong even when the numbers are identical.

climax.text: The trolley problem isn't just academic: triage medicine, self-driving cars, & military ethics all face exactly this.

punchline.text: Math says pull the lever. Your gut says don't push the man.

quiz.question: Why do most people approve of pulling the lever but not pushing the man, even though the numbers are identical?
options: Personal physical violence triggers stronger moral intuitions than impersonal actions

details.summary: The trolley problem asks whether it is moral to divert a runaway trolley to kill one person instead of five. This thought experiment reveals deep conflicts between utilitarian and deontological moral intuitions.
details.whyItMatters: Trolley-type dilemmas appear in real technology decisions like self-driving car algorithms, medical triage, and military targeting.
takeaways: Most people switch the trolley but refuse to push someone onto the tracks
The gap exposes tension between outcomes and personal responsibility
The problem has real applications in AI and autonomous vehicles

faq.question: Why do people respond differently to the trolley switch versus the footbridge?
faq.answer: Pushing someone feels like intentional killing via direct physical force, while flipping a switch feels more impersonal. The distinction highlights the role of personal involvement in moral judgment.

faq.question: Is the trolley problem useful beyond philosophy classrooms?
faq.answer: Yes. Autonomous vehicle programmers, hospital ethicists, and military planners face structurally similar dilemmas about how to weigh lives against each other.
